content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified air pollution as a significant global health threat, contributing to millions of deaths and years of lost healthy life annually. The burden of disease caused by air pollution is now comparable to other major global health risks, such as unhealthy diets and tobacco smoking. Air pollution is recognized as the largest environmental threat to human health. Despite some improvements in air quality in high-income countries, the global health toll from air pollution has not significantly declined since the 1990s. In contrast, air quality has worsened in many lowand middle-income countries due to rapid urbanization and economic development. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), such as cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological conditions, have become the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. Air pollution exacerbates these conditions, increasing morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, lung cancer, and potentially other organ system effects. The economic burden of air pollution-related diseases is also substantial, prompting governments to take action to improve air quality and reduce associated public health costs. The most recent update to these guidelines was published in 2021, following the last major update in 2006. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for managing air quality, including specific concentration levels for key pollutants such as particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone (O3), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and carbon monoxide (CO). The updated guidelines reflect advances in scientific evidence, including studies showing health effects of air pollution at lower levels than previously recognized. They also incorporate new methods for evidence synthesis and guideline development. While the guidelines are not legally binding, they serve as a critical tool for WHO Member States to inform legislation and policy. The ultimate goal is to reduce air pollutant levels and alleviate the significant health burden caused by air pollution worldwide. The guidelines also include interim targets to guide countries with high pollution levels toward achieving the recommended air quality levels over time. These targets are designed to be realistic and achievable within specific timeframes, serving as steps toward the ultimate goal of meeting the air quality guideline levels. Additionally, the guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring and managing specific types of particulate matter, such as black carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles from sand and dust storms, for which evidence is still emerging. The guidelines apply to both outdoor and indoor environments globally, covering all settings where people spend time. The target audience for these guidelines includes policymakers, lawmakers, technical experts, national and local authorities, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and researchers. The guidelines also highlight the need for collaboration across sectors and stakeholders to reduce air pollution and protect public health. Implementation of the guidelines requires robust air pollution monitoring systems, public access to air quality data, legally binding air quality standards, and effective air quality management systems. Gradual progress, marked by achieving interim targets, is essential for improving health outcomes in populations exposed to high levels of air pollution.
